Chemistry

 Home
OurBigBook.com Words: 171k Articles: 5k
Chemistry connects the composition and structure of chemical substances to their properties and transformations. Its central surprise is that rearranging the same chemical atoms can produce a different substance: molecular hydrogen and molecular oxygen can become water without changing which chemical elements are present. Chemical bonds explain the connections; chemical reactions describe the transformations; stoichiometry makes quantitative predictions from the bookkeeping.
This gives a useful route from an invisible world to measurable quantities. A molecule has a definite composition, such as two hydrogen chemical atoms and one oxygen chemical atom in water. A sample contains an enormous number of such molecules. Counting them through amount of substance, measured in moles, lets the same small-number ratios describe a macroscopic sample. The beauty is that the bookkeeping survives this huge change of scale.

Atmospheric chemistry

Words: 2k Articles: 55
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
The chemistry of gases, particles and droplets in planetary atmospheres. Chemical conversion competes with radiation, transport, mixing and removal to surfaces, so local equilibrium is not a general assumption.

HOx radical family (HOx​)

Words: 34
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
In the usual atmospheric convention, hydroxyl radical and HO2 form a rapidly interconverting hydrogen-oxide radical family. Some budgets also explicitly include H; state the counting convention. Radical production, recycling and termination differ from the abundance of the water reservoir.

Iodine monoxide (IO)

Words: 20
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A reactive iodine oxide radical. Its gas-phase abundance need not represent total reactive iodine when particulate reservoirs and multiphase recycling are important.

Climate-methane chemical-lifetime feedback

Words: 40
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
Changes in temperature, water vapor and radical chemistry alter methane removal. Warming can increase its hydroxyl radical reaction coefficient and the hydroxyl radical source from oxygen singlet D atom plus water, tending to reduce chemical lifetime at fixed precursor conditions. Changed emissions and competing radical sinks can modify or reverse that conditional response.

Tropospheric OH budget ([OH]=P/K)

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A local or box-model balance between hydroxyl-radical production and effective losses. For fixed production P and pseudo-first-order total loss frequency K, [OH]=P/K. Additional hydrogen, carbon monoxide or methane consumption can lower hydroxyl radical if production and other terms stay fixed; radical recycling and spatial transport can alter that simple result.

Hydrogen-induced methane lifetime response

Words: 41
Tropospheric OH budget OurBigBook.com
In a fixed-production hydroxyl radical box, adding hydrogen by Δ[H2​] changes K to K+kH2​+OH​Δ[H2​]. Methane lifetime scales as K/P when its hydroxyl radical reaction coefficient is held fixed. The pre-existing hydrogen contribution is already in K and must not be counted again.

Humidity-temperature response of OH production

Words: 43
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
At fixed relative humidity and fixed excited-oxygen concentration, a water-reaction hydroxyl radical source scales as es​(T)/T when concentrations are number densities. Thus dlnPOH​/dT=ΔHvap​/(RT2)−1/T under constant latent heat and rate coefficient. Using only es​ instead gives a vapor pressure or fixed-pressure mole-fraction approximation. Neither derivative follows without a humidity condition.

Dobson unit (DU)

Words: 28
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A unit of atmospheric column abundance. One Dobson unit corresponds to approximately 2.69×1016 molecules per square centimetre. Multiplying a column decrement by an absorption cross section gives its contribution to a monochromatic optical-depth decrement.

Bromine monoxide (BrO)

Words: 29
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
The radical BrO participates in catalytic atmospheric ozone destruction. Its measured abundance is only one partition of the total bromine inventory; precursor delivery, photodissociation and reservoir reactions determine the relation between the two.

Mixed chlorine-bromine ozone-loss cycle

Words: 52
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
In the productive mixed-radical pathway, chlorine monoxide and BrO yield chlorine and bromine atoms; subsequent atom reactions with ozone regenerate the oxides. The net cycle consumes two ozone molecules per radical-pair event, giving L=2k[ClO][BrO] when the subsequent steps are fast. The branching of a real chlorine monoxide–BrO reaction must be included if not already absorbed into its specified effective rate coefficient.

Chlorine nitrate (ClONO2​)

Words: 44
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
The reservoir species ClONO2​, formed from ClO and NO2 with third-body stabilization. Heterogeneous reaction with hydrogen chloride can produce molecular chlorine and nitric acid, activating chlorine while removing reactive nitrogen from the gas phase. It belongs to the wider reactive nitrogen family, not to the narrow NO-plus-NO2 definition of NOx.

Air-sea gas exchange

Words: 47
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
Transfer of a gas across the atmosphere–ocean interface, driven by a departure from the gas's interfacial equilibrium and controlled by transfer resistances and mixing. This can move an added atmospheric carbon-dioxide perturbation into the ocean without immediately returning all of that carbon to a permanent geological store.

Chlorine monoxide dimer cycle (ClO+ClO+M⇌ClOOCl+M)

Words: 130 Articles: 2
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A low-temperature catalytic ozone destruction pathway involving ClO association to ClOOCl, photodissociation of the dimer and regeneration of chlorine atoms. Combined with two Cl + O3 reactions its net effect is 2O3​→3O2​. Low temperature suppresses thermal dimer dissociation, while sunlight is needed for the photolytic step. Polar stratospheric clouds can activate reservoir chlorine before the sunlit cycle becomes rapid.

Photolytic branching in the chlorine dimer cycle (f=J/(J+kd​[M]))

Words: 38
Chlorine monoxide dimer cycle OurBigBook.com
For dimer photodissociation frequency J and competing thermal dissociation frequency kd​[M], the successful branch fraction is f=J/(J+kd​[M]). With steady dimer abundance and rapid subsequent recycling, ozone destruction is 2fka​[M][ClO]2. The factor two counts ozone molecules consumed per productive dimer event.

Chlorine peroxide (ClOOCl)

Words: 38
Chlorine monoxide dimer cycle OurBigBook.com
The peroxy-linked chlorine oxide ClOOCl, often written Cl2​O2​ in a chlorine monoxide dimer cycle. Thermal return to two chlorine monoxide radicals competes with a photolytic pathway that ultimately yields two chlorine atoms. The formula alone should not be taken as specifying every possible dichlorine-dioxide isomer.

Dry deposition

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
Removal of a gas or particle to a surface without precipitation. A simple parameterization uses downward flux F=vd​C, where C is the concentration near the surface and vd​ the deposition velocity. For a well-mixed layer of depth H, the loss is first order with coefficient vd​/H.

Deposition velocity (vd​=F/C)

Words: 36
Dry deposition OurBigBook.com
The ratio of a specified downward dry deposition flux to its reference near-surface concentration. It has units of speed but need not be an actual particle settling speed: transfer resistance and surface uptake can both control gas dry deposition.

Volatile organic compound

Words: 35
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
An organic compound readily present in the gas phase under the conditions of interest. In polluted-air chemistry, its oxidation can generate peroxy radicals which convert nitrogen monoxide to nitrogen dioxide without consuming ozone. Volatility alone does not determine reactivity or ozone yield.

Chlorofluorocarbon

Words: 28
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A compound composed of carbon, chlorine and fluorine, with no hydrogen. Many such fully halogenated molecules resist lower-atmospheric attack but release reactive chlorine after stratospheric photodissociation, contributing to catalytic ozone destruction.

Ozone-depletion potential (ODP)

Words: 46
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A relative measure of stratospheric ozone destruction associated with emissions of a substance, conventionally referenced to CFC-11. It depends on atmospheric survival, transport, halogen delivery and catalytic effectiveness, not only the number of chlorine atoms in the formula. Fluorine-only replacements can have negligible direct ozone-depletion potential while remaining strong greenhouse gases.

Atmospheric lifetime (τ)

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
For a well-mixed atmospheric burden B removed by a single first-order sink, dB/dt=−B/τ, the atmospheric lifetime is the exponential decay time τ. At steady emission rate E, this model gives B=Eτ. Independent sinks acting on the same burden have additive inverse lifetimes. Local removal times in separate compartments cannot be combined this way without considering exchange and partitioning. A multi-reservoir perturbation, especially atmospheric carbon dioxide, generally needs more than one timescale.

Methane perturbation lifetime

Words: 40
Atmospheric lifetime OurBigBook.com
The e-folding relaxation time of an added methane burden after accounting for chemical feedbacks. It need not equal burden divided by the contemporaneous methane loss rate: extra methane can consume hydroxyl radical and reduce its own removal. A fixed-OH exponential estimate omits that coupled adjustment.

Aerosol

Words: 561 Articles: 12
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com

Aerosol coagulation

Words: 44
Aerosol OurBigBook.com
Growth by collision and attachment of existing particles. Coagulation reduces particle number while conserving particulate material in a closed system without other sources or sinks. Larger particles can have a different scattering-per-mass efficiency and faster sedimentation, so increasing precursor injection need not increase albedo proportionally.

Sulfate aerosol

Words: 29
Aerosol OurBigBook.com
Atmospheric particles containing sulfate, commonly in sulfuric-acid/water or neutralized-salt mixtures. Particle size, water uptake, acidity and accompanying material determine scattering, absorption, cloud activation and heterogeneous chemistry; sulfate mass alone does not specify radiative forcing.

Aerosol hygroscopicity (κ)

Words: 47
Aerosol OurBigBook.com
A particle's tendency to take up water vapor, which depends on composition, solubility and ambient humidity. In a common parameterization, a dimensionless κ summarizes soluble-water uptake for use with dry diameter in Köhler theory. A single composition parameter does not remove the importance of particle size or parcel supersaturation.

Aerosol-cloud interaction

Words: 179 Articles: 3
Aerosol OurBigBook.com
A change in cloud microphysics or cloud properties caused by aerosol, including droplet activation, precipitation changes and adjustments of water content or coverage. The Twomey effect isolates a fixed-water-content optical response; it does not by itself establish the sign or magnitude of every cloud adjustment.
Semi-direct aerosol effect
Words: 44
Aerosol-cloud interaction OurBigBook.com
Cloud changes caused by aerosol absorption of radiation and the resulting heating. Heating can evaporate clouds and reduce shortwave reflection, but the effect can reverse when heating changes stability and cloud maintenance differently. The forcing sign depends on the relative positions of cloud and absorbing aerosol and on dynamical adjustment.
Twomey effect
Words: 96 Articles: 1
Aerosol-cloud interaction OurBigBook.com
Increasing cloud droplet number at fixed liquid-water content and cloud thickness reduces mean droplet size and increases total extinction area, raising shortwave optical depth and cloud albedo. This idealized response produces negative shortwave radiative forcing. Changes in cloud amount, water content and dynamics are separate adjustments.[ref]
Cloud albedo susceptibility (dA/dNd​=A(1−A)/(3Nd​))
Words: 55
Twomey effect OurBigBook.com
For τ∝Nd1/3​ at fixed liquid-water content and thickness, and A=τ/(τ+7), the derivative is dA/dNd​=A(1−A)/(3Nd​). For a fixed fractional number increase, the initial response is greatest at A=1/2. The exact finite-change expression is A′=sA/(1−A+sA) with s=(Nd′​/Nd​)1/3. Uncertain activation of additional particles and changes in water content limit direct application to real clouds.

Cloud condensation nucleus

Words: 262 Articles: 4
Aerosol OurBigBook.com
An aerosol particle able to activate into a growing cloud droplet at the supersaturation attained by a cloud parcel. Activity depends on particle dry size, hygroscopicity and interfacial properties. The number active at a specified supersaturation differs from total aerosol number.
Köhler theory
Words: 226 Articles: 3
Cloud condensation nucleus OurBigBook.com
The equilibrium water-vapor saturation ratio above a solution droplet combines a curvature effect, which raises vapor pressure, with dissolved-solute reduction of water activity. Its maximum defines a critical supersaturation for activation. In a dilute hygroscopicity approximation using droplet diameter D and dry diameter Dd​, s(D)≃AK​/D−κDd3​/D3, where AK​=4σMw​/(RTρw​). Then sc​≃4AK3​/(27κDd3​)​. These approximate forms assume the stated diameter convention and dilute solution; composition and surface tension must be consistent.[ref]
Radius and diameter conventions in Köhler activation
Words: 40
Köhler theory OurBigBook.com
Writing the same curve using diameter D=2r changes its coefficients: AD​=2Ar​ and BD​=8Br​ in AD​/D−BD​/D3. The critical saturation ratio is unchanged, while Dc​=2rc​. Mixing a diameter curvature coefficient with a radius solute term gives a spurious activation threshold.
Critical supersaturation (sc​)
Words: 109 Articles: 1
Köhler theory OurBigBook.com
The maximum equilibrium supersaturation along a solution-droplet growth curve. Above this threshold, an aerosol particle can grow into an activated cloud droplet under the conditions of the parcel. In Köhler theory, larger dry diameter or greater hygroscopicity generally lowers the threshold; aerosol number alone does not specify it.
Köhler activation radius (rc​=3B/A​,lnSc​=2A/(3rc​))
Words: 66
Critical supersaturation OurBigBook.com
In the dilute radius form lnSeq​=A/r−B/r3, the curvature coefficient A has length units and B has volume units. Setting its derivative to zero gives the displayed maximum. Ambient supersaturation above it permits activation into a growing cloud droplet. Below it, a sufficiently small wet equilibrium can be stable, while the larger-radius intersection is unstable. The approximation should not be extrapolated into the dry core.

Nitrogen oxides (NOx​)

Words: 77 Articles: 2
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
In the atmospheric convention used here, NOx​ denotes nitric oxide plus nitrogen dioxide. The broader reactive-nitrogen family NOy​ includes additional oxidized reservoirs; the chosen nitrogen-atom counting convention must be specified.

Nitrogen dioxide (NO2​)

Words: 25
Nitrogen oxides OurBigBook.com
The atmospheric nitrogen oxide NO2​. Daylight photodissociation forms nitrogen monoxide and an oxygen atom; subsequent third-body recombination with oxygen forms ozone. Whether this makes net ozone depends on the pathway that regenerated nitrogen dioxide.

Nitrogen monoxide (NO)

Words: 22
Nitrogen oxides OurBigBook.com
The atmospheric nitrogen oxide NO. It consumes ozone when converted to nitrogen dioxide by NO+O3​→NO2​+O2​, but its oxidation by peroxy radicals instead enables net photochemical ozone production.

Odd oxygen (Ox​=O+O3​)

Words: 144 Articles: 2
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A chemical-family bookkeeping variable in a simple stratospheric model. Interconversion of atomic oxygen and ozone preserves this count, while O+O3​→2O2​ removes two units. The definition must be extended consistently when including additional reservoirs or excited atomic states.

Chapman cycle

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Odd oxygen OurBigBook.com
A basic oxygen–ozone mechanism combining oxygen photodissociation, three-body ozone formation, ozone photodissociation and O+O3​→2O2​. The last reaction removes two units of odd oxygen; a catalytic cycle can add another loss pathway.
Temperature sensitivity of a catalytic ozone balance (dln[O3​]/d(T−1))
Words: 70
Chapman cycle OurBigBook.com
Suppose a reduced steady balance is P=AX2+BX, where X=[O3​], and hold P and all specified background concentrations fixed. With u=1/T, dlnA/du=−a and dlnB/du=−b, implicit differentiation gives dlnX/du=(aAX2+bBX)/(2AX2+BX). The quadratic loss term includes temperature-dependent O/O3 partitioning as well as the direct reaction coefficient. Holding the loss ratio fixed over a finite change is an additional approximation; solving the new quadratic provides a check.

Atmospheric mixing ratio (xi​=ni​/nair​)

Words: 42
Atmospheric chemistry OurBigBook.com
A number or mole fraction relative to a specified atmospheric reference population. For ideal gas partial pressures with a consistent wet/dry convention, xi​=pi​/p. A quoted ppm or ppb must state whether it denotes this number fraction, rather than a mass fraction.

Supramolecular chemistry

Words: 385 Articles: 16
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
The study and construction of molecular assemblies held together through noncovalent interactions, including recognition, host–guest complexes and self-assembly.

Chemical fuel

Words: 17
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
A reactant consumed irreversibly to drive a transient or maintained chemical state away from its unfuelled equilibrium.

Subcomponent self-assembly

Words: 25
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
Reversible formation of covalent ligands and metal coordination bonds from simpler components in the same mixture. imine condensation around a metal template is a common example.

Dissipative self-assembly

Words: 33
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
Assembly maintained or transiently created by consumption of a chemical fuel. A fuel-triggered state can decay as the fuel is irreversibly converted to waste, even though rapid binding equilibria hold within each instantaneous composition.

Self-sorting

Words: 50 Articles: 1
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
Selective distribution of components among preferred assemblies from a mixture. Competition, concentration, solvent and protonation determine the distribution; a ranking of individual affinities does not imply perfectly pure species.

Homochiral self-sorting

Words: 22
Self-sorting OurBigBook.com
Preferential assembly of components with matching handedness into an individual assembly. A racemic sample can contain equal populations of homochiral enantiomeric cages.

Dynamic covalent chemistry

Words: 48 Articles: 1
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
Use of reversible covalent bond formation and exchange to let molecular connectivities reorganize. A template can shift the equilibrium library, provided exchange remains kinetically accessible.

Disulfide exchange

Words: 23
Dynamic covalent chemistry OurBigBook.com
Interchange of sulfur substituents through reactions such as thiolate attack on a disulfide. Rates and equilibria depend on protonation, solvent and redox conditions.

Triazolophane

Words: 24
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
A macrocycle containing triazole and other linking units. Appropriate inward-directed C–H donors can bind anions cooperatively; cavity size and molecular preorganization can produce strong halide selectivity.

Molecular preorganization

Words: 27
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
Restriction of a host or reactant towards a binding- or reaction-competent geometry before association. It can reduce a conformational penalty but may decrease adaptability to other guests.

Cation–π interaction

Words: 24
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
A noncovalent attraction between a cation and an electron-rich aromatic system, with electrostatic and polarization contributions. Its solution free energy depends strongly on solvation.

Host–guest complex

Words: 121 Articles: 5
Supramolecular chemistry OurBigBook.com
A molecular association in which a host provides a binding site or cavity for a guest. Its equilibrium constant includes solvent and entropy contributions, not only direct host–guest attraction.

Cryptand

Words: 14
Host–guest complex OurBigBook.com
A molecular host with a three-dimensional cavity enclosed by several covalently connected donor-bearing bridges.

Crown ether

Words: 51 Articles: 2
Host–guest complex OurBigBook.com
A cyclic polyether host that can coordinate cations with inward-directed oxygen donors. Selectivity depends on donor arrangement, solvent and guest size, not ring size alone.
Aza-15-crown-5
Words: 17
Crown ether OurBigBook.com
A fifteen-membered crown with one nitrogen donor and four oxygen donors; nitrogen substitution can attach a signaling group.

Photoexcitation can dissociate a carbonyl ligand, creating a coordinatively unsaturated metal fragment. Capture by solvent or a tethered donor competes with CO recombination; net substitution therefore depends on both the photochemical step and subsequent trapping.

Different distributions of water between the metal coordination sphere and lattice for the same overall composition. Geometrical isomers can occur within one hydration class.

The square-planar coordination compound cis-diamminedichloroplatinum(II), with Pt(II), a d8 metal configuration and a 16-electron local valence count. This article concerns its coordination chemistry.

The Dewar-Chatt-Duncanson model describes an alkene–metal bond through donation from the filled alkene π orbital to the metal and pi backbonding from the metal into alkene π∗. A metal cluster contains several connected metal centers. A triangular three-metal cluster can support three edge metal-metal bonds; early-metal clusters often have stable counts below the 18-electron rule.

Chelation binds multiple donor sites of one ligand to the same central atom, forming a chelate ring. It can retain a donor near a metal even when one attachment temporarily opens.

A coordination ligand that coordinates one metal through three donor atoms. A facial tridentate donor set occupies the vertices of one face of an octahedron.

Enhanced complex stability associated with donor sites being held in a macrocycle, relative to comparable open-chain ligands. The comparison depends on donor geometry, solvation and strain.

The donor–metal–donor angle imposed by a chelating ligand. Tether length, ring conformation, donor distances and substituent crowding all influence it.

Chelation OurBigBook.com
The chelate effect is the enhanced stability often associated with binding several donor sites from one ligand compared with comparable independent donors. A chelate ring is a closed bonded path containing the central atom and a ligand with multiple attachments to it. A tethered Cp–pyridyl ligand can close such a path when the pyridyl N coordinates.

The trans effect is a kinetic influence whereby a ligand accelerates substitution opposite itself, classically in square-planar complexes. It must be distinguished from ground-state bond weakening and from the carbonyl cis effect.

Coordination chemistry OurBigBook.com
Electron counting records metal valence electrons plus ligand donations using a declared convention. In ionic counting, subtract metal oxidation state from its group number, then add donor electrons; in neutral counting, combine neutral metal and ligand fragments consistently. An Fe–Fe single bond contributes one electron to the count at each metal.

Electron counting OurBigBook.com
The 18-electron rule is a useful closed-shell guideline for many low-valent transition-metal complexes, filling nine valence orbitals. It is not universal: many early-metal d0 complexes have fewer electrons, while stable square-planar d8 complexes are often 16-electron.

A ligand field describes how ligands split and mix the central metal orbitals. Sigma donation, pi donation and pi backbonding explain trends that a purely electrostatic picture misses.

A parameter in a compact description of intra-atomic electron repulsion within a configuration. B and C control relative d-shell multiplet energies; B is not the octahedral splitting or a rotational constant.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
A plot of many-electron ligand-field term energies relative to the ground state against a normalized ligand-field strength. Axes commonly use E/B and Δo​/B, with the ratio of other interelectronic parameters stipulated. A change of ground-state term can create a break in the plotted reference.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
A model in which six donor orbitals of an octahedral complex form a1g​+eg​+t1u​ symmetry-adapted combinations. metal s, p and two d orbitals supply matching symmetry partners; the other three d orbitals remain nonbonding t2g​ orbitals. The model neglects ligand pi donation, backbonding and departures from octahedral symmetry.

Orbital energy barycentre

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
The degeneracy-weighted mean energy of a specified group of orbitals, ε=∑i​gi​εi​/∑i​gi​. Keeping it fixed separates level splitting from a common energy shift.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
A qualitative d-orbital splitting in a square-planar environment, with the strongly in-plane antibonding dx2−y2​ orbital highest. Ordering among the remaining orbitals can depend on the ligand set.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
The energetic cost assigned to pairing electrons in an orbital rather than placing them in distinct orbitals within a specified ligand-field model.

Spin crossover interconverts electronic states with different total spin, often in response to temperature. For octahedral iron(II), t2g4​eg2​ and t2g6​ correspond to S=2 and S=0. Ligand field OurBigBook.com
The electron pairing energy represents the energetic penalty for putting electrons into already occupied orbitals rather than suitable separate orbitals. A simple comparison with octahedral splitting explains high-spin and low-spin alternatives.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
A high-spin complex retains more unpaired electrons when the energy required for pairing exceeds the relevant orbital splitting. An octahedral high-spin d6 center has t2g4​eg2​ and S=2.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
The Jahn-Teller effect is an instability of a nonlinear molecular arrangement with an orbitally degenerate electronic ground state toward a symmetry-lowering distortion. An octahedral high-spin d4 ion has unequal occupation of its eg​ orbitals and often undergoes tetragonal elongation.

Words: 65
Jahn-Teller effect OurBigBook.com
For a real nonmagnetic electronic multiplet, a vibrational coordinate can couple linearly through a real symmetric electronic operator only if its representation occurs in the symmetric square. Remove the fully symmetric component when asking about symmetry-lowering distortion. In Td​, both Sym2T1​ and Sym2T2​ equal A1​+E+T2​, so E and T2​ modes are symmetry-eligible for either triplet; coupling strengths are not determined by this decomposition.

Jahn-Teller effect OurBigBook.com
A symmetry-lowering change separating two axial metal–ligand distances from four equatorial ones. Occupancy of the split orbitals determines the electronic energy gain, while elastic cost and pre-existing ligand asymmetry affect the observed structure.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
Crystal field theory models the effect of surrounding ligand charges or dipoles on metal atomic orbitals. Directional repulsion splits the d levels. Unlike molecular orbital theory, the simplest model does not explicitly construct covalent metal–ligand bonds.

Words: 24
Crystal field theory OurBigBook.com
Separation of metal d-orbital energies by the electrostatic field of surrounding coordination ligands. An octahedral field puts the three t2g​ orbitals below the two eg​ orbitals.
Tetrahedral crystal field splitting (Δt​)
Words: 91
Crystal field theory OurBigBook.com
In the ideal tetrahedral point-charge model, the five metal d orbitals split into a lower twofold e set and an upper threefold t2​ set. Relative to their weighted barycentre their energies are −3Δt​/5 and +2Δt​/5, where Δt​>0 is the separation. For occupancies ene​t2nt​​, the crystal field stabilization energy is (−0.6ne​+0.4nt​)Δt​. Under weak-field high-spin filling it is −0.6Δt​, −1.2Δt​, −0.8Δt​ and zero for d6,d7,d8,d10 respectively. Shorter metal–ligand distances generally increase the splitting, so orbital filling can superimpose nonmonotonic bond-length changes on an ionic-size trend. The model alone does not determine an absolute bond length.
Crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE)

The change in d-electron energy relative to the unsplit barycentre in a crystal-field model, before separately accounting for pairing and other bonding contributions.

A low-spin complex has the smaller-spin occupancy favored when ligand-field splitting outweighs the cost of pairing electrons in the lower orbitals. An octahedral low-spin d6 center has t2g6​eg0​ and total spin zero.

Ligand field OurBigBook.com
The spectrochemical series orders ligands empirically by the splitting they produce in comparable complexes. Pi-donor ligands tend toward smaller splittings and pi-acceptor ligands toward larger ones. Ligand field OurBigBook.com
In an ideal octahedral molecular geometry, the metal d orbitals divide into lower t2g​ and higher eg​ sets. Their separation is Δo​. Whether electrons pair in the lower set depends on that separation relative to pairing costs; observed many-electron transition energies need not equal Δo​ exactly.

Linkage isomerism occurs when complexes have the same composition but an ambidentate ligand attaches through different atoms. N-bound and O-bound nitrite provide the classical example. A linkage isomer is one member of a set exhibiting linkage isomerism, such as the N-bound or O-bound form of a coordinated nitrite.

A ligand in coordination chemistry is an atom, ion or molecule attached to a central atom through one or more donor sites. This use is distinct from a protein-binding ligand. A neutral CO ligand and an anionic chloride ligand can both donate two electrons in ionic electron counting.

A free radical monoanion intermediate in redox state between a quinone and a catecholate; an isolated ligand has spin S=1/2. Its spin may couple to a metal spin in a complex.

The dianionic, closed-shell O,O donor obtained by two deprotonations of catechol.

A nitrosyl shared between metal centres. In the simple mu2 counting model it contributes three electrons overall in the neutral method, or can be represented as an NO− donor of four electrons overall in ionic counting.

A coordinated aryne. Strong metal-to-aryne electron transfer can make a dianionic metallacyclopropene description more useful than an unreduced neutral alkyne description.

A ligand attached through an alkene carbon, commonly an X-type ligand in electron counting.

Radical (chemistry)

Words: 1k Articles: 24
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
A radical has one or more unpaired electrons. In a simple atomic orbital or molecular orbital occupancy picture, an unpaired electron occupies a spatial orbital without an opposite-spin partner in that orbital. A dot such as H∙ marks this electronic property; it does not mean a missing electron or positive electric charge. Free radicals can be neutral or charged. Terminology also has a boundary: metal ions exhibiting paramagnetism are not normally called free radicals just because they have unpaired electrons.[ref]
Compare three species containing the same single proton. The hydrogen atom H∙ has one electron in its 1s atomic orbital, and is a neutral radical. The hydrogen cation H+ has no electrons, so no unpaired electron. The hydrogen anion H− has two electrons paired in its 1s atomic orbital. It is charged but is not a radical in its ground state. With Np​ protons, Ne​ electrons, and positive elementary charge e, the independent electric charge count is
q=(Np​−Ne​)e;H+:q=+e,H∙:q=0,H−:q=−e.
(1)
The electron pair and electric charge questions require different information. An odd Ne​ ensures that not all electrons can be paired; an even Ne​ alone does not ensure pairing, as the molecular orbital description of molecular oxygen illustrates.
The distinction matters whenever a chemical reaction mechanism uses dots and charge signs together. Homolysis gives one bonding electron to each fragment, while heterolysis assigns both to one fragment. A radical chain reaction can pass an unpaired electron from one species to another without generating net electric charge. Detection then exploits the unpaired electron's spin and magnetic moment, rather than merely measuring whether the sample carries an electric charge.

Methane chlorination chain

Radical chain reaction OurBigBook.com
Light initiates methane chlorination by photodissociation of Cl2​ through homolysis. The elementary bookkeeping is
initiation:propagation:​Cl2​hν​2Cl∙,Cl∙+CH4​⟶HCl+CH3​∙,CH3​∙+Cl2​⟶CH3​Cl+Cl∙.​
(2)
Here hν denotes the photon energy. The first propagation step replaces a chlorine radical with a methyl radical; the second regenerates a chlorine radical. Adding the two propagation equations cancels both free radicals and gives CH4​+Cl2​⟶CH3​Cl+HCl: chloromethane and hydrogen chloride are made while the chain carrier is regenerated.[ref]
For example, recombination 2CH3​∙⟶C2​H6​ of methyl radicals makes ethane and a covalent bond from two unpaired electrons, removing two carriers. Recombination of two Cl∙ also terminates carriers; in the gas phase, stabilization of the product requires disposal of released energy, for example to a third collision partner. The figure omits that partner. Termination competes with propagation, and further chlorination can consume chloromethane, so this cycle alone does not predict a pure product or a measured reaction rate.[ref]

Stable radical

Words: 509 Articles: 2
Radical (chemistry) OurBigBook.com
An unpaired electron does not set a universal reaction rate. A stable radical can retain radical character during isolation and storage under specified conditions; a persistent radical survives long enough under specified conditions to be observed. These descriptions concern lifetime and handling, rather than immunity to every possible chemical reaction. DPPH is a practical counterexample to the claim that all free radicals react immediately.
Two mechanisms help explain persistence. Spreading electronic character over several chemical atoms, represented by chemical resonance, can lower the energy relative to a localized description. Bulky surrounding groups can impede approach to a reactive site and slow recombination. Lower energy and slower chemical kinetics are different advantages: neither alone guarantees a long lifetime. A primary computational study explicitly separates these effects, using electronic and geometric descriptors; it does not directly measure every predicted lifetime.[ref]

2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl

Words: 351 Articles: 1
Stable radical OurBigBook.com
DPPH is a neutral organic radical used as a spin reference in electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), also called electron spin resonance (ESR). Its unpaired electron remains bound within the chemical species: “free radical” does not mean a freely moving electron. The DPPH electron spin resonance experiment makes its magnetic moment observable.
DPPH electron spin resonance experiment
Words: 312
2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl OurBigBook.com
The University of Iowa's Electron Spin Resonance, University of Iowa laboratory protocol (revised July 2007, Experiment and Resonance Data Analysis, printed pp. 2–6) specifies DPPH on cotton in a tube inside an RF coil, between Helmholtz coils. A bridge monitors RF absorption; an oscilloscope records this output and the voltage across a 1Ω current-monitor resistor. Sweeping the coil current passes through the resonant magnetic field. The protocol describes two dips when the sweep revisits resonance; these are repeated crossings, not two distinct spectral lines.
Its calibration replaces the sample with a Hall effect probe, maps the magnetic field in 2mm steps, and accounts for sample dimensions. At least four RF frequencies test the resonance relation. Sweep speed is adjusted to obtain comparable passages. Only a local peak-plus-background fit is prescribed, because the full shape is not Gaussian. The protocol also flags unexplained trailing spikes and possible electronics contributions. These controls constrain field and sweep errors; an empty-tube/cotton blank would be an additional background control, not a reported measurement in this protocol.[ref]
For an isolated effective spin one-half with dimensionless positive factor g, the basic resonance model is
ΔE=gμB​∣B∣=hν,g=μB​∣Bres​∣hν​.
(3)
Here μB​ is the Bohr magneton, h is the Planck constant, ν is the applied frequency, and Bres​ is the calibrated resonant magnetic field. A change in frequency should shift the resonance field proportionally in this model. The factor g describes the electronic magnetic moment coupling, not the species' net electric charge.
A resonance supports the presence of detectable paramagnetism. It does not, by itself, identify an unknown radical: other species exhibiting paramagnetism, impurities, overlapping responses, and interactions with atomic nuclei can complicate interpretation. Conversely, absence of a detectable resonance need not mean absence of free radicals; a low concentration, a short lifetime, or an unsuitable measurement range can conceal them. The occupancy and chain diagrams are original bookkeeping illustrations; neither is a measured or simulated DPPH spectrum.

Density functional theory

Quantum chemistry OurBigBook.com
A framework describing electronic ground-state properties using the electron density. Practical approximations require an exchange-correlation functional; this does not mean that explicit electrons have been replaced by a classical atom-only force field.

Exchange-correlation functional (Exc​[n]=F[n]−Ts​[n]−EH​[n])

Words: 58
Density functional theory OurBigBook.com
The part of the exact density functional left after subtracting the auxiliary noninteracting kinetic energy and classical Hartree electrostatic energy. It includes fermionic exchange, correlation and the difference between interacting and noninteracting kinetic energies. Its functional derivative enters the Kohn-Sham equations. Practical approximations to this functional, rather than the existence of a density description itself, are a central source of error.

Density functional variational principle (E0​=minn​{F[n]+∫vn})

Words: 58
Density functional theory OurBigBook.com
The constrained-search functional F[n]=minΨ→n​⟨Ψ∣T+W∣Ψ⟩ is universal for a fixed interaction. Minimization of F[n]+∫vn over admissible densities with the correct electron number gives the ground-state energy. Each trial density represents a constrained set of antisymmetric states, so minimizing over densities and their representing states recovers the ordinary variational principle. The admissible domain and possible degeneracy must be handled explicitly.

At fixed total density the exchange term favors spin polarization, whereas the kinetic term opposes it.

Expanding near P=0 gives a quadratic coefficient 5/9−r/2, so the unpolarized state first loses local stability at r=10/9. The endpoint crossing is therefore not the actual continuous onset; intermediate polarizations matter.

Hund's rules

Words: 184 Articles: 1
Electron configuration OurBigBook.com
Friedrich Hund's rules describe the usual ground-term ordering within an atomic electron configuration in the LS coupling regime. First maximize the total spin S subject to the Pauli exclusion principle. Among the terms with that spin, maximize total orbital angular momentum L. Within the resulting term, the lowest level has J=∣L−S∣ for a less-than-half-filled open subshell and J=L+S for a more-than-half-filled one. These are ordering rules, not universal replacements for diagonalizing an arbitrary atomic Hamiltonian operator.
For two equivalent p electrons, parallel spins give S=1. Their spatial wavefunction must be antisymmetric; the highest allowed orbital projection with parallel spins is 1+0=1, giving L=1. A p2 subshell is less than half filled, so its lowest term symbol is 3P0​, followed within that term by 3P1​ and 3P2​. Closed subshells contribute zero total L and S.

An effective local exchange coupling can favor parallel electron spins in different orbitals on the same atom. The displayed sign convention represents that preference. It underlies the high-spin tendency in Hund's rules and the alignment of itinerant and core spins used in double exchange. The coupling is an effective description of intra-atomic Coulomb and exchange energies, rather than a separate classical magnetic force.

An atomic orbital is a one-electron spatial wavefunction used to describe an electron's state in a chemical atom. A normalized atomic orbital has ∫∣ϕ∣2d3r=1, and the Born rule gives the position probability density ∣ϕ∣2. It is a function extending through space, not a prescribed classical orbit. [ref]
The linear combination of atomic orbitals combines these single-centre functions to approximate a molecular orbital. The orbital overlap measures their inner product, and their relative quantum phase controls the interference shown in molecular orbital theory.

Molecular orbital theory

Words: 2k Articles: 31
Quantum chemistry OurBigBook.com
Molecular orbital theory describes the electronic arrangement of a molecule using molecular orbitals: one-electron spatial wavefunctions extending over the combined atomic nuclei. Filling bonding molecular orbitals can stabilize a chemical bond; filling antibonding molecular orbitals opposes that stabilization. A molecular orbital is a building block of a many-electron description, rather than the entire many-electron wavefunction. See Robert W. Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 24, pp. 1–4: molecular orbitals and the LCAO approximation.
First make the interference visible with an exactly normalized one-dimensional toy. Replace the three-dimensional 1s atomic orbitals of the hydrogen atom by two Gaussian functions centred at x=±a, with dimensionless x and a>0:
ϕA​(x)=π−1/4e−(x+a)2/2,ϕB​(x)=π−1/4e−(x−a)2/2,S=∫−∞∞​ϕA​ϕB​dx=e−a2.
(4)
The normalized sum and difference are ψ±​=(ϕA​±ϕB​)/2(1±S)​, following the same linear combination of atomic orbitals algebra. At a=1, the orbital overlap is S=e−1≈0.367879. At the midpoint, ϕA​(0)=ϕB​(0)≈0.455581, giving
ψ+​(0)≈0.550879,∣ψ+​(0)∣2≈0.303468,ψ−​(0)=∣ψ−​(0)∣2=0.
(5)
Both probability densities have total integral one: interference redistributes probability, rather than creating an extra electron. These are toy wavefunctions, not actual hydrogen atom orbitals or predictions of molecular hydrogen energies.
Now fill the two 1s-derived molecular orbitals in the minimal model. The lower bonding molecular orbital is labelled σg​; the upper antibonding molecular orbital is σu∗​. The Pauli exclusion principle permits at most two electrons in each spatial molecular orbital, with opposite spin projections along a chosen axis. For the lowest electron configuration in this model, fill σg​ first. The subscripts g and u denote even and odd behaviour under inversion through the midpoint; the star marks an antibonding molecular orbital. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, 8.4: occupancy and bond order and Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 25, pp. 1–3: bonding, antibonding, and symmetry labels.
With Nb​ electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and Na​ in antibonding molecular orbitals, the model's bond order is b=(Nb​−Na​)/2. The three elementary counts are:
  • Molecular hydrogen, H2​: two electrons give (σg​)2 and b=(2−0)/2=1.
  • The hydrogen molecular ion H2+​: one electron gives (σg​)1 and b=(1−0)/2=1/2.
  • Two neutral helium chemical atoms, He2​: four electrons give (σg​)2(σu∗​)2 and b=(2−2)/2=0 in this minimal 1s model.
The zero bond order says this minimal model gives no net covalent bond for He2​. It does not rule out every bound pair of helium chemical atoms: a very weak Van der Waals force can bind a neutral helium dimer, which has been observed experimentally. See Zeller et al., Imaging the He2 quantum halo state using a free electron laser, PNAS 113, 14651–14655 (2016), p. 14651: van der Waals binding and Luo et al., The weakest bond: Experimental observation of helium dimer, Journal of Chemical Physics 98, 3564–3567 (1993). The bond order count does not include that weak binding mechanism.
The useful surprise is that sharing alone does not determine a chemical bond: the relative quantum phase and the occupancy matter together. The same two shapes explain why adding an electron to a bonding molecular orbital increases the model's bond order, while adding one to an antibonding molecular orbital decreases it. Molecular orbital theory also accounts for the unpaired electrons and paramagnetism of molecular oxygen, which its all-paired Lewis structure misses. See Chemistry 2e, 8.4: the molecular orbital description of oxygen.

A diagram linking reactant and product orbitals by a symmetry conserved along a stipulated reaction path. Orbitals of the same symmetry avoid crossing in a generic one-parameter problem; orbitals of different symmetry can cross. Correlation constrains connectivity, not quantitative barrier heights.

Mixing between symmetry-compatible s-derived and p-derived orbital combinations. It shifts energies and changes orbital shapes; in a centrosymmetric diatomic, gerade and ungerade combinations do not mix with one another.

Hückel method

Words: 523 Articles: 9
Molecular orbital theory OurBigBook.com
A model of conjugated π molecular orbitals with an orthonormal atomic basis, one-centre energies αi​, and resonance matrix elements βij​ between selected neighbouring sites. Solving Hc=Ec gives orbital energies and coefficients. Its simplicity makes symmetry and electron filling explicit, but quantitative charge predictions can depend strongly on the chosen parameters and omitted orbital relaxation.
Cube nearest-neighbour Hückel model (E−α∈{3β,β,−β,−3β})
Words: 90
Hückel method OurBigBook.com
With one orthonormal site orbital per cube vertex, common site energy α, and coupling β along every edge, the one-electron Hamiltonian is αI+βA, where A is the cube adjacency matrix. Its eigenvalues are α+3β,α+β,α−β,α−3β with multiplicities 1,3,3,1.
One proof labels each vertex by three signs. The adjacency operator flips one sign at a time, so a product of k coordinate signs is an eigenfunction of A with eigenvalue 3−2k. There are (k3​) such products. For β<0, eight electrons fill the lowest four spatial molecular orbitals, yielding total one-electron energy 8α+12β.
Hückel square-to-trapezium distortion
Words: 102
Hückel method OurBigBook.com
For a four-site cycle with site energy α, three resonance integrals β<0 and one weakened integral nβ, 0<n<1, put D=(n−1)2+4​. In the independent-electron Hückel method, filling the two or four lowest spin orbitals gives total electronic energies E2​=2α+β(n+1+D) and E4​=4α+2βD. At the square limit n=1, these become 2α+4β and 4α+4β. The weakened-edge distortion raises the two-electron sum but lowers the four-electron sum. Near n=1 the latter change is β(1−n)2/2+O((1−n)4), so its first-order term cancels. This electronic comparison omits structural repulsion and other restoring forces, and does not determine the open-shell spin at the square limit.

For a bipartite pi system with a common diagonal energy α, the orbital spectrum is paired about α. If H=αI+K and P changes the sign on one sublattice, then PKP=−K; an eigenvector of energy α+ϵ is mapped to one of energy α−ϵ. Their site-probability magnitudes are equal.

For real orthonormal site functions, pij​=∑k​fk​cik​cjk​, where fk​ is orbital occupation. It measures the off-diagonal pi density matrix; a complete C–C bond also contains a sigma contribution.

The diagonal one-centre energy αi​ assigned to a pi-basis orbital. This one-electron parameter is distinct from a two-electron Coulomb repulsion integral in Hartree-Fock theory.

An off-diagonal Hamiltonian matrix element between selected neighbouring pi-basis functions. The usual bonding convention has β<0; non-neighbour matrix elements are neglected.

With equal on-site energy α and equal pair interaction β<0, the three-site Hamiltonian has one eigenvalue α+2β and a degenerate pair α−β. This model explains symmetry and filling but omits ingredients needed for a quantitative dissociation energy.

The change in energy on allowing a specified localized orbital reference to delocalize across a conjugated system. In a Hückel method calculation, the reference must use the same one-centre parameters and bond types as the delocalized molecule. With the signed convention Eπ​−Elocalized​, stabilization is negative; its positive magnitude is often also called the delocalization energy, so the sign convention must be stated.

In an orthonormal Hückel method basis, an occupied molecular orbital with occupancy fk​ contributes fk​∣cik​∣2 electrons to site i. Adding one electron to a fixed orbital changes the site population by ∣ci​∣2. A coefficient sign indicates orbital phase, not charge sign. A net atomic charge also needs a reference population and treatment of the electrons outside the model.

Words: 653 Articles: 12
Molecular orbital theory OurBigBook.com
A molecular orbital is a one-electron spatial wavefunction for the combined atomic nuclei of a molecule. For a normalized molecular orbital, the Born rule gives the position probability density ∣ψ(r)∣2, with ∫R3​∣ψ∣2d3r=1. The molecular orbital is the amplitude, rather than its squared modulus or a classical trajectory.
In the independent-orbital approximation, a doubly occupied molecular orbital contributes 2∣ψ∣2 to the electron number density, whose integral is two. An empty molecular orbital contributes zero, even though its shape is still part of the model. The molecular hydrogen example therefore uses one occupied spatial molecular orbital for two electrons, distinguished by their spins. A negative real probability amplitude means a relative quantum phase of π, not positive electric charge; multiplying the whole wavefunction by −1 changes only its global phase.

Molecular orbital OurBigBook.com
A molecular orbital near the boundary between occupied and unoccupied levels. The highest occupied molecular orbital and LUMO are central examples. Their energies, occupancies, spatial form and symmetry help predict which new chemical bonds can form when fragments approach.

A molecular orbital whose occupation changes bonding between the selected centres relatively little. In a real complex, weak bonding or antibonding contributions may replace exact nonbonding character.

For an open-shell species, distinguish a singly occupied spatial orbital from a vacant spin orbital. Adding an electron to an oxygen molecule can fill the opposite-spin vacancy in a pi-star singly occupied molecular orbital even though the next completely empty spatial orbital is sigma-star.

A spatial molecular orbital occupied by one electron. In an open-shell molecule, its empty opposite-spin slot can accept another electron even though the spatial orbital is occupied.

A molecular orbital with little or no net bonding interaction between the atoms in the stated orbital model. A mainly localized lone pair can acquire bonding admixture when a distortion permits additional mixing.

An energy-level scheme showing the occupied molecular orbitals and their relation to atomic orbitals. Occupancies must account for degeneracy and spin.

In pyramidal ammonia, the hydrogen symmetry orbitals span A1​⊕E of the C3v molecular point group. Nitrogen 2s and 2pz​ both have A1​ symmetry and (2px​,2py​) span E. In the planar D3h molecular point group, these become A1′​, A2′′​ and E′, respectively, while the hydrogen combinations span A1′​⊕E′. Molecular orbital OurBigBook.com
Occupying a bonding molecular orbital favours a chemical bond. For the two equivalent 1s atomic orbitals of the hydrogen atom, the sum σg​=σ+​ has constructive interference between the protons. The resulting electron density in that region helps stabilize the combined system. Its lower energy in this model follows from the Quantum Hamiltonian, not from the plus sign alone; see Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 25, pp. 1–2.
For example, (σg​)2 in molecular hydrogen supplies Nb​=2, hence bond order one when Na​=0. The sum in the molecular orbital theory toy has midpoint probability density 0.303468, whereas the difference has zero there. The normalization factors must be included in this comparison.

Molecular orbital OurBigBook.com
Occupying an antibonding molecular orbital opposes a chemical bond. For equivalent 1s atomic orbitals of the hydrogen atom, the difference σu∗​=σ−​ vanishes on the plane halfway between the protons: every point there is equally far from both centres, so the amplitudes cancel. This nodal plane removes the contribution of this molecular orbital to electron density on that plane; it does not make an entire finite region empty. The 1s-derived antibonding molecular orbital lies above its bonding molecular orbital partner in energy. See Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 25, pp. 1–2.
In the He2​ minimal model, (σu∗​)2 adds Na​=2 and cancels the bond order contribution of (σg​)2. Opposite signs on the two lobes describe probability amplitudes, while both lobes have nonnegative probability density after squaring. The star is an orbital label, not an extra electron or an electric charge.

The LCAO approximation builds a molecular orbital as a linear combination of single-centre atomic orbitals. For two equivalent normalized real 1s functions ϕA​ and ϕB​, choose their signs positive and define their orbital overlap S. At nonzero separation, 0<S<1, and the normalized combinations are
σ±​(r)=2(1±S)​ϕA​(r)±ϕB​(r)​,S=∫R3​ϕA​(r)ϕB​(r)d3r.
(6)
Here σ+​=σg​ and σ−​=σu∗​. Equal coefficients use the equivalence of the two centres; a general LCAO need not have equal coefficients. See Field, MIT 5.61, lecture 24, pp. 3–6: LCAO coefficients and overlap integrals.
For the Gaussian function toy's a=1, the two denominators are 2(1+S)​≈1.654013 and 2(1−S)​≈1.124385. To check wavefunction normalization, expand the square: ∫(ϕA​±ϕB​)2=1+1±2S. Dividing by 2(1±S) gives one. The local probability density is
∣σ±​∣2=2(1±S)ϕA2​+ϕB2​±2ϕA​ϕB​​.
(7)
The cross term is the interference; adding the separate densities first would lose it. These formulas normalize the chosen linear combination exactly, while the restricted choice of atomic orbitals remains an approximation to an actual molecular orbital.

The normalized equal sum is A1​; three coordinate-sign combinations span T2​. Every normalized coefficient vector has entries ±1/2 in a suitable orthonormal real basis. These functions simplify a Hamiltonian invariant under the tetrahedral operations, but equivalent symmetry copies on other sites may still mix.

For the Gaussian function toy, increasing a from 1 to 2 reduces S from e−1≈0.367879 to e−4≈0.018316. As S tends to zero, both LCAO normalization denominators tend to 2​.

Thus adding one electron to a bonding molecular orbital raises b by 1/2, while adding one to an antibonding molecular orbital lowers it by 1/2. The configurations drawn above give 1, 1/2, and 0. Molar mass (M)

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
Molar mass turns a weighed sample into a count of specified particles. For a pure chemical substance with specified chemical formula and isotopic abundances, its molar mass is
M=nm​,n=Mm​,
(8)
where m is the sample mass and n its amount of substance. The SI unit is kgmol−1; the common laboratory unit is gmol−1, with 1gmol−1=10−3kgmol−1. Equal values of amount of substance correspond to equal counts of specified entities, but heavier entities give greater masses.
Combining this definition with molecular count and amount of substance gives
N=MmNA​​,mˉparticle​=Nm​=NA​M​,NA​=6.02214076×1023mol−1.
(9)
The Avogadro constant is exact under the modern definition of the mole. The mass M/NA​ is the mean mass per specified entity; if isotopes differ within the sample, individual molecules need not all have that mean mass.[ref]
Specify what n counts: water molecules, hydrogen chemical atoms, and oxygen chemical atoms give different values of amount of substance for the same sample. For a mixture, dividing total mass by total amount of substance of its chosen entities gives a composition-dependent mean. A polymer sample can contain many chain molar masses; its number-average molar mass and weight-average molar mass answer different averaging questions. Relating either to degree of polymerization also requires a unit-mass convention and end-group accounting.

Number-average molar mass (Mn​)

Words: 23
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
The number-average molar mass weights each molecule equally. For counts ni​ with molar masses Mi​,
Mn​=∑i​ni​∑i​ni​Mi​​.
(10)
A mass-proportional SEC detector response requires conversion to counts before determining this average.

Weight-average molar mass (Mw​)

Words: 41
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
The weight-average molar mass weights each population by its contribution to total mass:
Mw​=∑i​ni​Mi​∑i​ni​Mi2​​.
(11)
Here ni​ counts molecules with molar mass Mi​. SEC light-scattering detection can infer this average for an eluting slice under its optical and concentration assumptions; overlapping species need not have the same individual molar mass.

Relative molecular mass (Mr​)

Words: 57
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
The relative molecular mass is the dimensionless ratio of a specified mean molecule mass to the unified atomic mass unit, written mu​ when treated as a physical quantity:
Mr​=mu​mˉmolecule​​,M=Mr​Mu​.
(12)
Thus a relative molecular mass of approximately 18.015 and a molar mass of approximately 18.015gmol−1 describe related quantities with different units. The conversion uses the molar mass constant, rather than identifying a dimensionless number with a mass per mole.

Molar mass constant (Mu​=NA​mu​)

Words: 66
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
The molar mass constant converts relative atomic mass or relative molecular mass into molar mass. It is approximately 1gmol−1. Its SI numerical value is determined experimentally: the exact Avogadro constant multiplies an experimentally determined unified atomic mass unit in kilograms. Treating Mu​ as exactly 1gmol−1 is therefore an excellent elementary-calculation approximation, rather than a defining equality of the modern SI.[ref]

Water mass to molecular count

Words: 193
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
Choose approximate atomic weights Ar​(H)=1.008 and Ar​(O)=15.999, and use Mu​≈1gmol−1. The chemical formula H2​O then gives water molar mass
M(H2​O)≈(2(1.008)+15.999)gmol−1=18.015gmol−1.
(13)
These are deliberately chosen rounded inputs, not exact atomic weights or a universal value for every water sample. Different isotopic abundances, notably those in heavy water, change the mean molar mass; chemical formula alone does not specify them. Adding atomic weights also neglects the tiny mass change associated with chemical bond energies, immaterial at this rounding precision.
For an illustrative pure water sample of mass 4.50375g, this convention gives
n≈18.015gmol−14.50375g​=0.250000mol,N≈1.50553519×1023.
(14)
The count refers to water molecules. Their hydrogen chemical atom count is approximately 2N=3.01107038×1023, and their oxygen chemical atom count is approximately N. The mean mass per water molecule is M/NA​≈2.99146×10−26kg. Extra displayed digits expose the arithmetic; they do not imply that the sample composition or mass was measured that precisely.
The same conversion makes stoichiometry a mass calculation. For the chemical equation 2H2​+O2​→2H2​O, complete conversion of 0.250000mol of molecular hydrogen and 0.125000mol of molecular oxygen gives 0.250000mol of water. With the chosen approximate atomic weights, the reactant masses are 0.50400g and 3.99975g, summing to 4.50375g. The 2:1:2 ratio belongs to molecule counts and amount of substance, not to masses; this bookkeeping neglects the much smaller reaction energy contribution to mass.

Words: 98
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
Suppose a synthetic polymer population contains three chains of molar mass 10000gmol−1 for every one chain of molar mass 40000gmol−1. Multiplying both chain counts by any common factor leaves the averages unchanged. Substitution into the existing number-average molar mass and weight-average molar mass definitions gives
Mn​=43(10000)+40000​gmol−1=17500gmol−1,Mw​=3(10000)+400003(10000)2+(40000)2​gmol−1≈27143gmol−1.
(15)
The larger chains are only one quarter of the chain count but supply 40000/70000=4/7 of the mass. Thus a weighted mean that emphasizes mass gives a larger result than one that weights each molecule equally. Total mass divided by total chain amount of substance gives Mn​, while Mw​/NA​ is not the mean mass of a randomly chosen chain. Inferring chain counts from size-exclusion chromatography still requires the existing SEC detector response and SEC molar mass calibration assumptions.

Vapor-density molar mass measurement

Words: 357 Articles: 1
Molar mass OurBigBook.com
An ideal gas law measurement obtains amount of substance without knowing the chemical formula in advance:
n=RTpV​,Minferred​=pVmRT​.
(16)
Here p is vapor pressure, V is its occupied volume, T is absolute temperature, R is the molar gas constant, and m is the mass of vapor occupying that volume at those conditions.
Santa Monica College's teaching experiment uses a 125mL Erlenmeyer flask with a pinhole foil cap, a 600mL water bath on a hot plate, a thermometer, and a barometer. Excess volatile liquid displaces air. A dissolved dye loses its colour and deposits when the liquid evaporates; three more minutes of heating follow. Cooling condenses retained vapor. Subtracting the dry assembly mass from the cooled assembly mass supplies m. The flask volume comes from brim-full water mass and mass density at its measured temperature. Controls include a dry exterior, excluding bath water, and three trials.[ref]
The inference assumes vapor pressure equals atmospheric pressure, vapor and bath reach thermal equilibrium, the retained vapor mass is recovered on cooling, and the vapor obeys the ideal gas law. Residual air, thermal expansion of the flask, and vapor temperature below bath temperature are explicit error questions in the teaching experiment. Repeating trials assesses repeatability; it does not remove a shared bias.[ref]

Molar mass measurement model

Words: 146
Vapor-density molar mass measurement OurBigBook.com
For a synthetic illustration, choose m=0.3000g, V=125.0mL, p=101325Pa and T=373.15K. Using molar gas constant R≈8.314462618Jmol−1K−1 gives n≈0.00408234mol and Minferred​≈73.4873gmol−1 under the ideal gas law. These are chosen model inputs, not observations of a particular chemical substance.
An error's direction follows the model. Extra exterior water raises the apparent m and hence Minferred​. If a fraction f of the hot gas particles is residual air, and only the unknown vapor contributes to recovered m, an otherwise ideal gas calculation gives Minferred​=(1−f)Mtrue​. For a pure nonideal vapor, define Z=pV/(nRT); then Minferred​=Mtrue​/Z, so the direction depends on Z. The dye endpoint alone cannot establish gas purity, thermal equilibrium, or ideality. These conditional checks explain why the same apparatus cannot provide a universal molar mass measurement for arbitrary mixtures or substances that decompose on heating.

Ion (q=ze)

Words: 1k Articles: 37
Chemistry OurBigBook.com
An ion is a chemical atom or a group of chemical atoms with a nonzero net electric charge. A positive ion is a cation; a negative ion is an anion. The whole entity carries the electric charge: a hydronium ion is a group of four chemical atoms with net charge +e. This definition agrees with [ref].
For an ordinary ion containing only atomic nuclei and electrons, let Np​ count all its protons and Ne​ all its electrons. Each proton contributes the elementary charge +e, each electron contributes −e, and neutrons contribute zero. Therefore
q=(Np​−Ne​)e=ze,z=Np​−Ne​.
(17)
The signed integer z is the net electric charge number. Removing an electron increases z by one; adding an electron decreases z by one. Changing the electron count leaves the atomic number, and therefore the identity of the chemical element, unchanged.
For example, a neutral sodium chemical atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. Its cation Na+ still has 11 protons, but only 10 electrons, so q=(11−10)e=+e. A neutral chlorine chemical atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons; its anion Cl− has 17 protons and 18 electrons, so q=(17−18)e=−e. These are particle inventories, not pictures of atomic orbitals. See 2.6 Ionic and Molecular Compounds (§2.6: ions and ionic compounds).
One sodium chloride formula unit accounts for one Na+ cation and one Cl− anion, whose net electric charges sum to zero. Ordinary solid sodium chloride is an extended arrangement of ions, rather than discrete NaCl molecules. This is a useful distinction: a neutral material can contain charged constituents, and its chemical formula tells us their ratio without claiming that each pair is a separate molecule.
Ion bookkeeping connects chemistry to electric current: moving ions can transport electric charge, while stationary ions cannot supply a transport current density. In electrochemistry, both signs of ions can contribute to the same conventional current. An ion opposing a fixed electric charge is called a counterion.

Kirchhoff's law of thermochemistry ((∂ΔH/∂T)p​=ΔCp​)

Thermochemistry OurBigBook.com
At fixed pressure, the temperature derivative of a reaction or transformation enthalpy is the corresponding difference in heat capacity at constant pressure:
(∂T∂ΔH​)p​=ΔCp​,ΔH(T2​)=ΔH(T1​)+∫T1​T2​​ΔCp​(T)dT.
(18)
Use a consistent molar or mass basis and retain each phase's range of stability when applying the relation.
